Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Although many people think of a heart attack as a painful, sometimes fatal event, there are some heart attacks that go entirely unnoticed. Some people may have had heart attacks without knowing it, studies show. Undiagnosed, or "silent," heart attacks affect nearly 200,000 people in the United States annually. As many as 40 to 60 percent of all heart attacks are unrecognized, studies show. By definition, a heart attack usually happens when a clot gets in the way of blood flow from a coronary artery to the heart. This may cause symptoms such as severe chest pain, shortness of breath, fainting and nausea. Anyone who believes that he or she is having a heart attack should seek emergency medical attention. But sometimes a heart attack is not painful, or the person experiencing it does not recognize the symptoms as heart-related, so he or she does not go to a hospital for treatment. Cardiologists have only recently become attuned to the prevalence of these silent heart attacks, and research on treatment is limited. The risk factors for silent heart attacks are the same as for regular heart attacks, experts say, and include smoking, diabetes, stress and family history.  Watch CNN Health Files: Heart attacks » . A new study from Duke University Medical Center shows that these silent heart attacks may occur more frequently than physicians thought. Even if a heart attack occurred in the distant past, it may still leave a signature called a Q-wave on an electrocardiogram. But there are silent heart attacks that do not have associated Q-waves. Researchers used a relatively new technique called delayed-enhancement cardiovascular magnetic resonance and then followed up with patients after about two years. The study was done on 185 patients who had never had a diagnosed heart attack but were suspected of having coronary artery disease. The researchers found that 35 percent of patients had evidence of a heart attack and that silent heart attacks without Q-waves were three times more common than those that had Q-waves. Patients with non-Q-wave silent heart attacks also had 11 times higher risk of death from any cause and a 17-fold risk of death from heart problems compared with patients without any heart damage. But experts do not recommend that people generally be screened for silent heart attacks unless they have other heart-related problems. "Currently, there has not been a study that has demonstrated that early identification and therapy changes how patients with unrecognized heart attacks do in the future," said Dr. Han Kim, a cardiologist at Duke University and lead author of the study. "If you don't know when an actual event occurred, it becomes difficult to prescribe therapy." Although the study was done on a relatively small sample of people at risk of coronary artery disease, meaning the results may not apply to the general population, other cardiologists say the study has merit in adding to the knowledge of silent heart attacks. "Ultimately, we're going to need trials to really establish what treatment works and what doesn't," said Dr. Eric Schelbert, a cardiologist at the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine who was not involved in the study. Treatment for someone who has had a silent heart attack is usually the same for someone who came to the hospital immediately after a heart attack, Kim said. This may include beta blockers, statin drugs, aspirin or other medications, Schelbert said. Schelbert said he has seen plenty of patients who have had silent heart attacks; in fact, he has treated some of his own colleagues who have experienced them. "It's an incredibly important thing that the physician scientist community needs to explore further," he said. Researchers noted that patients with non-Q-wave silent heart attacks were also generally older and were more likely to have diabetes. There needs to be more of a focus on prevention among these risk groups, said Dr. David Wiener, a cardiologist at the Thomas Jefferson University Hospital in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, who was not involved in the study.

(CNN) — Heart attacks are often imagined as intensely painful and potentially deadly episodes, yet some occur without the person ever realizing it. Research suggests that almost 200,000 Americans experience these undiagnosed, or “silent,” heart attacks each year. Studies estimate that 40% to 60% of all heart attacks may go unrecognized.

A heart attack generally occurs when a blood clot blocks circulation through a coronary artery to the heart. Typical warning signs can include severe chest discomfort, difficulty breathing, nausea and fainting. Anyone who suspects a heart attack should obtain emergency medical care immediately.

However, not every heart attack causes pain. In other cases, people may fail to identify their symptoms as heart-related and therefore never seek hospital treatment. Cardiologists have only recently begun to appreciate how common silent heart attacks may be, and evidence about how best to treat them remains limited.

According to experts, recognized and silent heart attacks share the same risk factors, including diabetes, smoking, stress and a family history of heart disease.

Watch CNN Health Files: Heart attacks »

Research from Duke University Medical Center indicates that unnoticed heart attacks could be more widespread than doctors previously believed. A heart attack—even one that happened long ago—can sometimes leave a distinctive pattern known as a Q-wave on an electrocardiogram. Some silent heart attacks, however, produce no Q-wave.

For the study, investigators used a relatively new imaging method called delayed-enhancement cardiovascular magnetic resonance. They examined 185 people who were thought to have coronary artery disease but had never been diagnosed with a heart attack, then followed them for approximately two years.

Evidence of a previous heart attack was detected in 35% of the participants. Silent heart attacks without Q-waves occurred three times as often as silent attacks that produced Q-waves. Compared with patients who showed no heart damage, those with non-Q-wave silent heart attacks had 11 times the risk of dying from any cause and 17 times the risk of dying from a heart-related condition.

Despite these findings, experts do not advise routine screening for silent heart attacks in the general population unless a person has other cardiac concerns.

“No study has yet shown that detecting an unrecognized heart attack early and changing treatment improves a patient’s future outcome,” said Dr. Han Kim, the study’s lead author and a cardiologist at Duke University. He added that choosing a treatment is difficult when doctors cannot determine when the event took place.

The research involved a fairly small group of people already at risk for coronary artery disease, so its conclusions may not extend to the population as a whole. Nevertheless, other cardiologists said the findings make a valuable contribution to what is known about silent heart attacks.

Dr. Eric Schelbert, a University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine cardiologist who did not participate in the research, said clinical trials will ultimately be necessary to determine which treatments are effective and which are not.

Kim said patients found to have had a silent heart attack are generally treated in the same way as those who seek hospital care immediately after a recognized attack. Schelbert said therapy may involve aspirin, statins, beta blockers or other drugs.

Schelbert has encountered many patients with previously unnoticed heart attacks, including some of his own professional colleagues. He described the issue as extremely important and said physician-scientists need to investigate it more thoroughly.

The researchers also found that patients with silent, non-Q-wave heart attacks tended to be older and were more likely to have diabetes. Dr. David Wiener, a cardiologist at Thomas Jefferson University Hospital in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, who was not involved with the study, said prevention efforts should receive greater emphasis among these higher-risk groups.

counterfactuals.output:
# Silent heart attacks may go unnoticed — but the damage can be serious

A heart attack does not always arrive with crushing chest pain or a dramatic collapse. In some people, the warning signs are mild, unusual or absent altogether — a condition commonly called a “silent” heart attack.

Like any heart attack, a silent myocardial infarction occurs when blood flow to part of the heart is blocked long enough to injure or kill heart muscle. The event may not be recognized at the time, but the resulting scar can increase the risk of heart failure, abnormal heart rhythms and another heart attack.

## Symptoms can be easy to dismiss

Despite the name, silent heart attacks may cause subtle symptoms, including:

- Pressure, tightness or mild discomfort in the chest  
- Shortness of breath  
- Unusual fatigue or weakness  
- Nausea, indigestion or upper-abdominal discomfort  
- Sweating, dizziness or lightheadedness  
- Pain in the back, jaw, neck or arms  
- A general sense that something is wrong  

People may mistake these symptoms for heartburn, a pulled muscle, anxiety, a viral illness or normal aging. Women, older adults and people with diabetes are more likely to experience atypical symptoms, although a silent heart attack can happen to anyone.

Anyone with new chest discomfort, breathing difficulty, cold sweats, faintness or pain spreading to the arm, jaw or back should seek emergency care immediately. Symptoms that improve should not be ignored.

## Who is at risk?

The risk factors are largely the same as those for a recognized heart attack:

- High blood pressure  
- High cholesterol  
- Diabetes  
- Smoking  
- Obesity and physical inactivity  
- Older age  
- A family history of early heart disease  
- Chronic kidney disease  
- Prior cardiovascular disease  

Diabetes is particularly important because nerve damage can blunt pain signals, making reduced blood flow to the heart less noticeable.

## Duke study found hidden heart damage

Research from Duke University Medical Center highlighted how often heart attacks can escape routine detection.

In a study of 185 people with suspected coronary artery disease but no known history of heart attack, cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, or MRI, identified previously unrecognized heart-muscle scarring in about 27% of participants. By comparison, electrocardiograms detected signs known as Q waves — a traditional marker of an earlier heart attack — in only about 8%.

During follow-up, patients with MRI evidence of an unrecognized heart attack faced substantially greater risks of death and major cardiovascular events. The findings suggested that small, non-Q-wave heart attacks may be missed by standard electrocardiograms but still carry serious prognostic consequences.

The study was observational and involved a selected group already being evaluated for possible coronary disease, so its results do not mean everyone should undergo cardiac MRI. They do, however, underscore that an unnoticed heart attack is not necessarily a harmless one.

## How doctors make the diagnosis

A silent heart attack may be discovered during evaluation for fatigue, shortness of breath or another problem — or years later during routine testing.

Doctors may use:

- **Electrocardiogram:** Looks for electrical patterns suggesting current or previous heart injury.  
- **Blood tests:** Cardiac troponin can reveal recent heart-muscle damage.  
- **Echocardiogram:** Shows how well the heart pumps and whether part of the muscle moves abnormally.  
- **Cardiac MRI:** Can identify scar tissue and provide a detailed view of heart-muscle injury.  
- **Stress testing or coronary imaging:** Helps determine whether narrowed arteries are limiting blood flow.

An ECG can miss some older or smaller heart attacks, so additional testing may be appropriate when symptoms or risk factors raise concern.

## Treatment focuses on preventing another event

If doctors discover a previous silent heart attack, treatment depends on the extent of damage and whether significant artery blockages remain. It may include:

- Aspirin or other antiplatelet medication when appropriate  
- Cholesterol-lowering statins  
- Blood-pressure medicines, including beta blockers or ACE inhibitors  
- Diabetes management  
- Smoking cessation  
- Regular physical activity and a heart-healthy diet  
- Cardiac rehabilitation  
- Angioplasty, stenting or bypass surgery for selected patients  

People should not begin aspirin on their own, because it can cause serious bleeding and is not appropriate for everyone.

The key message, heart specialists say, is that “silent” describes the symptoms — not the consequences. Recognizing personal risk factors, attending regular medical visits and responding quickly to even subtle warning signs can limit heart damage and potentially save a life.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Report on new research showing that undiagnosed non-Q-wave heart attacks may be more common and dangerous than doctors previously believed.
counterfactuals.output:
### Hidden non-Q-wave heart attacks may be more common—and more dangerous—than once thought

New research suggests that many heart attacks occur without producing the classic electrocardiogram pattern doctors traditionally used to identify them. These “non-Q-wave” or unrecognized myocardial infarctions can leave permanent heart damage and substantially increase a patient’s risk of heart failure, another heart attack, or death.

Unlike major heart attacks that create a prominent Q wave on an ECG, smaller or differently located attacks may cause subtle, temporary, or no obvious ECG changes. Symptoms can also be mild or atypical—such as fatigue, shortness of breath, indigestion, nausea, or back discomfort—so patients may never seek emergency care.

Studies using cardiac magnetic resonance imaging have found areas of scar tissue consistent with previous heart attacks in people who had never received that diagnosis. MRI can detect damage that a routine ECG misses, indicating that standard records may underestimate the true number of heart attacks.

The findings challenge the assumption that an unnoticed or non-Q-wave heart attack is relatively harmless. Even limited scarring can weaken the heart, disrupt its electrical system, and signal widespread coronary artery disease. Patients with previously unrecognized infarctions have shown worse long-term outcomes than people with no evidence of heart damage.

“Non-Q-wave” is an older term; doctors now generally classify acute attacks without persistent ST-segment elevation as non-ST-elevation myocardial infarctions, or NSTEMIs. The categories are not perfectly interchangeable, but both emphasize that the absence of classic ECG findings does not rule out serious injury.

Researchers are not recommending cardiac MRI screening for everyone because it is expensive and may lead to incidental findings. Instead, the work supports closer evaluation of people with cardiovascular risk factors or suspicious symptoms, using high-sensitivity troponin blood tests, repeat ECGs, echocardiography, coronary imaging, or MRI when clinically appropriate.

Anyone experiencing chest pressure, unexplained shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, sudden weakness, or pain in the arm, jaw, back, or upper abdomen should seek emergency care—even if the symptoms are mild or come and go.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a medical news story about “silent” heart attacks, citing statistics, expert cardiologists, study limitations, and recommendations regarding screening and prevention.
counterfactuals.output:
## “Silent” heart attacks may go unnoticed—but still carry lasting risks

A heart attack does not always arrive with crushing chest pain. Some cause mild, atypical symptoms—or none that a patient recognizes—and are discovered only later through an electrocardiogram, cardiac imaging or tests performed for another reason.

These so-called silent myocardial infarctions can still damage heart muscle and increase the risk of heart failure, another heart attack and death.

The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention estimates that about **one in five heart attacks is silent**, meaning the damage occurs without the person being aware of it. Estimates vary, however, depending on how researchers define a silent heart attack and whether they use electrocardiograms, blood tests or imaging to detect old damage.

In a 2016 analysis of **9,498 adults** in the long-running Atherosclerosis Risk in Communities study, researchers identified 703 heart attacks over a median of nearly nine years. Of those, **317—or about 45%—were classified as silent** because they appeared on follow-up electrocardiograms but had not been clinically diagnosed. Both silent and recognized heart attacks were associated with a higher risk of death, according to the study, published in *Circulation*.

“Silent myocardial infarction is not necessarily benign simply because it was not recognized when it happened,” said **Dr. Elsayed Z. Soliman**, a cardiologist and epidemiologist at Wake Forest University School of Medicine who led the study. His research has emphasized that finding evidence of a previous silent heart attack should prompt clinicians to reassess a patient’s cardiovascular risk and prevention plan.

### Symptoms can be subtle

“Silent” does not always mean completely symptom-free. People may dismiss pressure or discomfort in the chest, shortness of breath, nausea, sweating, unusual fatigue, heartburn-like discomfort, or pain in the back, jaw or arms. Symptoms may be especially easy to overlook in older adults and people with diabetes, who may have reduced pain sensation because of nerve damage.

**Dr. Martha Gulati**, a preventive cardiologist at Cedars-Sinai and a past president of the American Society for Preventive Cardiology, has cautioned that heart-attack symptoms do not look the same in everyone. Women can experience chest pain—the most common symptom in both sexes—but may also report shortness of breath, nausea or profound fatigue, which can be misattributed to stress, indigestion or another illness.

Anyone with new chest pressure, breathing difficulty, faintness, cold sweats or unexplained upper-body discomfort should seek emergency care rather than wait for symptoms to pass. In the United States, clinicians advise calling 911 because emergency medical teams can begin assessment and treatment en route to a hospital.

### Why routine screening remains controversial

Despite the potential consequences, major medical organizations do not recommend routinely screening every healthy, symptom-free adult with an electrocardiogram.

The **U.S. Preventive Services Task Force** recommends against screening low-risk, asymptomatic adults with resting or exercise ECGs to prevent cardiovascular events. For adults at intermediate or high risk, the task force has concluded that evidence is insufficient to determine whether routine ECG screening improves outcomes.

False-positive or unclear results can lead to stress tests, coronary angiography and other procedures that carry costs and potential harms. A normal ECG also cannot reliably exclude a previous heart attack: small infarctions may leave no lasting electrical pattern, and ECG abnormalities can fade over time.

More sensitive tests, including cardiac magnetic resonance imaging, can detect scar tissue that an ECG misses. But cardiac MRI is expensive, is not practical for population-wide screening and may reveal incidental findings of uncertain significance.

Instead, cardiologists generally recommend targeted evaluation for people with symptoms, known cardiovascular disease, abnormal examination findings or substantial risk factors. Testing may also be appropriate when an incidental ECG abnormality suggests an old infarction, but the result often requires confirmation because conditions other than a heart attack can mimic that pattern.

### Important limits to the evidence

The ARIC findings were observational, so they cannot prove that the silent infarctions themselves caused later deaths. The study also defined silent heart attacks using changes on periodic ECGs, a method that may miss some infarctions and misclassify others.

Participants were initially recruited from four U.S. communities and were middle-aged at enrollment, limiting how broadly the results can be applied. Differences reported by sex or race may also reflect access to care, underlying risk factors or statistical uncertainty rather than biology alone.

Research using cardiac MRI often finds a different prevalence because the technology detects smaller or differently located scars. For that reason, the CDC’s one-in-five estimate and the ARIC study’s 45% proportion should not be treated as contradictory: they come from different data sources and definitions.

### Prevention remains the main strategy

For most people without symptoms, experts say the priority is not searching for an old heart attack but reducing the chance of a first—or another—cardiovascular event.

Recommendations include:

- Checking and treating high blood pressure, cholesterol and diabetes.
- Avoiding tobacco and secondhand smoke.
- Getting regular physical activity, generally aiming for at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity exercise each week when medically appropriate.
- Eating a diet rich in vegetables, fruit, whole grains, legumes, nuts and fish while limiting sodium, refined carbohydrates and saturated fat.
- Maintaining a healthy weight and addressing sleep disorders.
- Discussing overall cardiovascular risk with a clinician, including family history.
- Using statins, blood-pressure drugs or other preventive medications when indicated.
- Not starting daily aspirin without medical advice, because bleeding risks can outweigh benefits in many people without established cardiovascular disease.

People found to have evidence of a previous heart attack may need further evaluation and secondary-prevention treatment. That can include cholesterol-lowering medication, blood-pressure control and, in selected patients, antiplatelet therapy—but treatment should be individualized after the diagnosis is confirmed.

**Sources:** CDC heart-attack information; Soliman EZ et al., *Circulation* (2016), ARIC study of silent myocardial infarction; U.S. Preventive Services Task Force recommendation on ECG screening; American Heart Association and American College of Cardiology prevention guidance.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Explain how heart attacks can go unnoticed and summarize the study of 185 coronary artery disease patients that found elevated mortality risks among those with non-Q-wave silent heart attacks.
counterfactuals.output:
A heart attack can go unnoticed when it causes no chest pain or only vague symptoms—fatigue, shortness of breath, nausea, sweating, back or jaw discomfort, or “indigestion.” These symptoms may be dismissed, particularly in older adults, women, and people with diabetes or impaired pain perception. Some infarctions also leave no classic **Q waves** on a routine electrocardiogram, so the event may remain undiagnosed even after the symptoms pass. Cardiac MRI with late gadolinium enhancement can later reveal the resulting scar.

### Study of 185 patients

Researchers studied **185 people with suspected coronary artery disease but no known previous myocardial infarction**, using ECG, coronary angiography, and contrast-enhanced cardiac MRI.

- MRI identified **non-Q-wave unrecognized infarctions in 50 patients (27%)**.
- By comparison, ECG identified Q-wave evidence of an old unrecognized infarction in only about **8%**.
- During a median follow-up of roughly **2.2 years**, **13 of the 50 patients** with a non-Q-wave silent infarction died, versus **3 of the other 135 patients**.
- The study reported that a non-Q-wave unrecognized infarction was associated with approximately an **11-fold higher risk of death from any cause** and a **17-fold higher risk of cardiac death**. The association remained important after accounting for other clinical and heart-function measures.

The study was relatively small and observational, so the exact risk estimates had wide uncertainty and do not prove causation. Nevertheless, it showed that “silent” does not mean harmless: MRI-detected non-Q-wave scars can mark substantial underlying coronary disease and a markedly worse prognosis.
